- Current provider (vendor X) end-to-end observed numbers (measured client->vendor->client from our EU region): p95 ≈ 500ms, p99 ≈ 900ms for typical short-chat flows (~20 prompt tokens / ~40 response tokens).

Tom / team —

A few technical notes ahead of the call + attached perf-test-plan.md (high level):

- Definitions: For our internal reporting we’ll produce:
  * TTFB (time-to-first-byte) — useful for streaming UX; this is what users perceive as responsiveness.
  * TTLB (time-to-last-byte) / end-to-end completion — used for throughput accounting and background tasks.
  * p95/p99 are statistically computed over the sample population for each metric.

- Streaming vs non-streaming: streaming improves perceived latency (TTFB) but can complicate p99 for TTLB if you rely on fewer big messages. For chat we recommend targeting TTFB p95 <= 150–250ms and TTLB p95 consistent with your UX tolerance.

- Batching tradeoffs: automatic continuous batching can reduce cost but increases TTFB for low-volume tenants. We can run tests in two modes: low-latency (no batching, single-request dispatch) and high-throughput (continuous batching with target micro-batch window).

- Measurement location: to isolate vendor processing we’ll run server-side timers at ingress/egress and also provide client-side synthetic measurements (from an EC2 in your region) so we can separate network tail from processing tail.

- Concurrency and resource planning: to hit p95 <=300ms at 80 concurrent active streams you’ll likely need dedicated capacity/optimized kernels for your chosen model family. We’ll propose a recommended config after the baseline.

Next: I’ll run an initial controlled benchmark this afternoon against our hosted endpoint using your token sizes and the streaming profile you described. Expect a raw results drop and summary within 24 hours.

Attachment: perf-test-plan.md

Cheers,
Rishi
